Chapter 12

A table as a log

Two append-only tables, enforced by triggers, and why SQLite is a defensible choice for the spine of an exchange.

By the end of this chapter

Build the log, and understand the three properties it actually needs.

A real venue's log lives in shared memory or Aeron and is measured in nanoseconds. Ours is a SQLite table. That choice is worth defending rather than apologising for.

A log needs exactly three properties: it must be durable, it must be totally ordered, and consumers must be able to resume from a position. A STRICT table with an explicit integer primary key in WAL mode has all three — plus one a message broker does not: you can SELECT * FROM command_log WHERE seq = 1834 during an incident and read the answer with your eyes.

What it does not have is throughput. Tens of thousands of appends a second, not tens of millions. For a teaching venue that is four orders of magnitude more than we need, and every idea in this part — sequencing, checkpointing, gap detection, idempotent consumers — transfers unchanged to the fast version.

The two tables

The SQL lives inside a String.raw template literal in schema.ts rather than in a .sql file — the file's header tells the story of the production build that could not find schema.sql — which is why every backtick in its comments is preceded by a backslash.

STRICT is SQLite 3.37+. Without it, SQLite will happily store the string "banana" in an INTEGER column, because its type system is advisory by default. With it, that is an error. For a system of record, advisory typing is not enough.

Append-only, enforced

The log is append-only. Not "we agreed not to update it" — enforced.

Why a trigger rather than a code review rule

At 3am during an incident, somebody will want to "just fix that one row". They will have a good reason. The trigger means they cannot, and have to fix it the way that leaves a trail — by appending a correction. Every enforcement that lives only in people's heads is an enforcement that fails under pressure, which is exactly when it matters.

The pragmas, and one that must not be in a batch

Three of the four settings are properties of the connection, not the database, and since @libsql/client 0.18 a client is not one connection but a small pool of them. A statement outside a transaction borrows a connection and hands it back before its promise resolves, so four execute calls in a row all land on the *same* connection — and the other three turn up later with whatever the library compiled in. busy_timeout has a client option that reaches every connection. The other two do not, so they are applied the only way that addresses each connection individually: by holding all of them at once.

How many connections that is, is a decision of its own:

Why four, and why not one

One is the size that looks safest and is the only one that breaks. A transaction holds its connection for its whole life, and when transactions hold every connection the pool refuses the next borrower with TRANSACTION_ACTIVE rather than making it wait. With one connection, every read that arrives while a write is in flight throws — and in the web process that is a live query polling while an order is appended, which is to say constantly. Two is the floor. Four leaves room for a stray direct client.transaction() somewhere without starving the readers. More buys nothing: a statement outside a transaction borrows a connection, runs synchronously and returns it before anything else in the process can run, so reads never genuinely overlap inside one Node process, and each extra connection is two more file descriptors held open for nothing.

Two details carry the weight, and the doc comment on configurePool spells both out. PRAGMA foreign_keys is a documented no-op inside a transaction, so each held connection first runs ROLLBACK — there is nothing to roll back — and then the pragmas, in one executeMultiple: the one method on a transaction that does not check the transaction is still open between statements. Then close() hands the configured connection back to the pool, where it is reused ahead of any new one. An in-memory database or a remote libSQL server is not a pool this can reach, so it takes the plain branch at the top and the pragmas run once.

The connection-level settings are the ones that fail silently. A process that forgets busy_timeout is the one that fails under load with SQLITE_BUSY while every other process is fine; a connection that misses foreign_keys is the one that lets an event point at a command that never happened. Both are maddening to debug precisely because the other connections are fine. That is why every process in Sequent calls one openStore function rather than creating clients itself, and why there is a test that reads the settings back through every connection in the pool.

A test needs a value that could have been different

The first version of that test read busy_timeout, foreign_keys and synchronous back through every connection and expected 5000, 1 and 2. It passed — and it passed just as well with configurePool reduced to an immediate return, because the timeout comes from the client option and libSQL compiles in the other two as its defaults. An assertion that agrees with the defaults cannot tell configured from forgotten. So openStore takes connectionPragmas, which nothing in the venue uses, and the test opens a store with PRAGMA cache_size = -4321 — a value nobody would choose and no build has as its default — and finds it on all POOL_SIZE connections. With configurePool stubbed out it reads -2000, and fails, which is the property a test is for.

Checkpoint

  • You can name the three properties a log needs
  • You can explain why seq is not an autoincrement in command_log
  • You can explain why the WAL pragma cannot go in a batch
  • You know why the append-only rule is a trigger
